slides.say: How many diagonals does an eight-sided polygon have?
This question type is rare, but it does show up on the exam. A diagonal joins two vertices that are not next to each other. So a side is not a diagonal.
We'll solve it in four different ways. Let's start with the simplest math way. We draw it, and we count. Exam polygons are small, so drawing and counting is a real option.
Here are the eight vertices and the eight sides.
From vertex one, we draw a line to every vertex that is not next to it. Vertex one has five diagonals.
From vertex two, also five new diagonals.
From vertex three, four new ones, because the diagonal to vertex one is already drawn.
Then three, two and one new diagonals from the next vertices.
Five plus five plus four plus three plus two plus one is twenty diagonals. With eight sides it's already crowded, so let's see faster ways.
[pause] Now the second way, with mutual action. A line between two vertices is a mutual action. The line from one to two is the same as the line from two to one.
We count as usual. Eight vertices to start from, and seven others to go to. Eight times seven is fifty-six.
Every line was counted from both ends, so we divide by two. Fifty-six divided by two is twenty-eight lines.
But twenty-eight is all the lines, and eight of them are the sides of the polygon. Sides are not diagonals. That's why twenty-eight, choice number one, is a trap.
at: choice number one, is a trap

slides.say: Twenty-eight minus eight is twenty diagonals.
[pause] The third way is like the drawing in the lesson. From the first vertex, seven new lines. From the next one, six new lines, then five, four, three, two and one.
Each time it's one fewer, because one line already came from the vertex before. Seven plus six plus five plus four plus three plus two plus one is twenty-eight lines.
Again, eight of those lines are sides. Twenty-eight minus eight is twenty.
[pause] And the fourth way, a formula. The number of diagonals is n times n minus three, divided by two.

slides: Why minus three? From each vertex there's no diagonal to itself, and none to its two neighbours. So each vertex has n minus three diagonals. And we divide by two, because each diagonal has two ends.

slides.say: Here n is eight. Eight times five is forty.
Careful, forty is choice number four, and it's a trap. Forty counts every diagonal from both of its ends.
Forty divided by two is twenty. Four ways, and one answer.
Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number two is our answer
